newsitem.title: USA: California sounds caution on tobacco pact.
newsitem.headline: California sounds caution on tobacco pact.

text.p: California Attorney General Dan Lungren hailed a proposed agreement Friday between state negotiators and the tobacco industry but warned that California would only participate in a settlement that "appropriately reimburses" state taxpayers.
State negotiators earlier announced an agreement with the tobacco industry on a landmark settlement of many legal claims and tobacco-related public health issues.

"The agreement in principle ... is the first step toward an historical global settlement that will justly compensate California's taxpayers and force the tobacco industry to deal truthfully with the public about the harm their products can and have caused," Lungren, a Republican, said in a statement.

"This agreement presents the opportunity to accomplish much more in terms of good public policy than the alternative: an endless series of courtroom battles across the nation," he said, adding that the agreement would permanently change the way the tobacco industry does business.
But Lungren warned that California, the most populous state, "will only participate in a settlement that appropriately reimburses the taxpayers of our state."
"As it is presently constructed, this agreement will settle California's claims as represented in the lawsuit I filed against the industry last week," he said.

Lungren said he and other state attorneys general would be meeting in Wyoming next week. "Several of my top lawyers will accompany me as we look forward to working there to ensure that the final agreement, including the allocation formula for settlement monies to the states, protects California's interests," he said.

California joined the list of states suing the tobacco industry to recover the cost of health care for smoking-related illnesses on June 12. The state's suit sought to recover medical expenses of about $433 million incurred by the state for each of the past three years.
Lungren announced the lawsuit after Gov. Pete Wilson signed legislation amending a 1987 state law that had shielded tobacco companies from product liability suits.
